new_groups.label: The embargo laws
new_groups.definition: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807 and the acts of the first session of the Tenth Congress that extended it, enforced it and allowed the President to suspend it, as the 1808 papers printed them, most of them 'by authority': the supplementary act of 9 January, the additional act of 12 March, the act of 22 April authorising a suspension and the act of 25 April. Contains those five groups. Only 1808 printings are included; the Embargo Act was first printed in December 1807.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Embargo Act of 22 December 1807
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 22 December 1807 laying an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbors of the United States: no clearance for a foreign port, and bonds for coasting vessels. This group holds the act's 1808 printings; it was first printed in late December 1807, and those printings are not included.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The supplementary act of 9 January
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 9 January 1808 supplementary to the Embargo Act: vessels licensed for the coasting trade, and fishing and whaling vessels, may not depart without bond that they will not go to a foreign port, with penalties for evading the embargo.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The additional act of 12 March
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 12 March 1808 in addition to the supplementary act: no boat that is neither registered nor licensed, and no foreign vessel, may depart, and goods may not be exported from the United States by land or by water.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act allowing the President to suspend the embargo
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 22 April 1808 authorising the President, during the recess of Congress, to suspend the embargo in whole or in part if peace, a suspension of hostilities or changes in the belligerents' measures made American commerce sufficiently safe.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act of 25 April enforcing the embargo
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 25 April 1808 in addition to the embargo acts: vessels whose trade is confined to bays, sounds, rivers and lakes must give bond, and collectors may detain vessels and unusual deposits of goods suspected of evading the embargo.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Charges against General Wilkinson, 1808
new_groups.definition: Documents and reports of the charges that General James Wilkinson had taken money from the Spanish government, as the 1808 papers printed them: his challenge to John Randolph and Randolph's answer (December 1807), Daniel Clark's statement to the House, the President's message of 20 January, and the opinion of the military court of inquiry (printed from 4 July). Contains those four groups. The statement and the letters are allegations and each writer's own account; the court found no evidence.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Wilkinson's challenge and Randolph's answer
new_groups.definition: Printings of two letters of 24 and 25 December 1807, from a pamphlet: General James Wilkinson asks John Randolph, a member of the House, for satisfaction for words injurious to his reputation, and Randolph refuses. Each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Daniel Clark's statement to the House
new_groups.definition: Printings of the statement of Daniel Clark, delegate from the Territory of Orleans, laid before the House on 11 January 1808 and sworn before Judge Cranch: that General Wilkinson had dealings with the Spanish government and received money from it. It is an allegation.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 20 January on Wilkinson
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to the House of 20 January 1808, answering its resolutions of 13 January on General Wilkinson: a court of inquiry, asked for by Wilkinson, was already sitting, and he reported what the executive's records held on foreign intrigues and on any corrupt receipt of money by an officer of the United States.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The court of inquiry's opinion on Wilkinson
new_groups.definition: Printings of the opinion of the military court of inquiry at Washington on General Wilkinson (signed by its president, Colonel Burbeck, and approved by the President), printed from 4 July 1808: it found no evidence that Wilkinson had received a pension or money from the Spanish government for corrupt purposes.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Orders and decrees against neutral trade
new_groups.definition: Three measures of the warring powers against neutral commerce, as American papers printed them in the first half of 1808: the British Order in Council of 11 November 1807, a merchant house's account of Napoleon's Milan decree, and the British instructions of 11 April 1808 on provisions for the West Indies. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British Order in Council of 11 November 1807
new_groups.definition: Printings of the order of the King in Council of 11 November 1807 that put the ports of France and her allies, and every port from which the British flag was excluded, under the restrictions of a blockade, as retaliation for the French decrees.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: An Amsterdam letter on the Milan decree
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Daniel Crommelin and Sons, Amsterdam, 30 December 1807, received at New York on 13 February 1808: official news of a decree of the French Emperor at Milan under which vessels that had submitted to British search or paid duties in Britain were to be treated as denationalised. It is a merchant house's summary, not the decree.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: British instructions of 11 April on provisions for the colonies
new_groups.definition: Printings of the King's instructions to the commanders of British ships of war and privateers (Windsor, 11 April 1808): they were not to interrupt neutral vessels laden with lumber and provisions bound to the British colonies, under the conditions the instructions set.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Algiers and the American ships, 1808
new_groups.definition: A New Bedford report of February 1808 that Algiers had declared war on the United States, the American consul general's circular of the same weeks that the dispute was settled, and a June report of the Dey's new demands. Contains those three groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New Bedford: 'War with Algiers'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New Bedford handbill of 30 January 1808: the ship Honestus, 42 days from the Downs, had been told off Cape Trafalgar that Algiers had declared war against America and captured American vessels. It is a report; the consul general's circular, printed in the same weeks, says the dispute had been settled.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lear's circular: peace with Algiers
new_groups.definition: Printings of the circular of Tobias Lear, American consul general at Algiers (16 December 1807), received at Salem in February 1808: three American vessels detained by an Algerine frigate, because the annuities were two years in arrears, had been released after he settled with the Dey.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Washington: the Dey of Algiers makes new demands
new_groups.definition: Printings of a National Intelligencer paragraph of 24 June 1808 ('We understand'): after the settlement of December, the Dey had demanded in March two thousand dollars a man for Algerine seamen lost in the rescue of a captured American vessel, threatening to put Consul Lear in chains. It is a report from the government's paper.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message on more troops, February 1808
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of February 1808 (communicated on 26 February) recommending an increase of the military force, regular and volunteer, with the Secretary of War's letter proposing new regiments; the message and the letter are one publication, counted once.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lisbon under the French, December 1807
new_groups.definition: Printings of news from Lisbon papers of December 1807, brought by the brig Perseverance: decrees of the French general in chief after the occupation, forbidding the use of arms to all but the military, confiscating English property and making French and Spanish money current.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British and French papers laid before Congress, 1808
new_groups.definition: The President's message of 22 March 1808 and the correspondence with Britain and France it laid before Congress, as the papers printed it from March to May: Canning and Monroe on the Chesapeake (No. II), the letters of George Rose and James Madison on Rose's mission (No. III), and Champagny's letter to Armstrong of 15 January, made public on 2 April. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 22 March
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message of 22 March 1808 laying before Congress the correspondence with Britain on the Chesapeake, the unratified treaty and Rose's mission, and with France.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Canning and Monroe on the Chesapeake
new_groups.definition: Printings of the correspondence between George Canning and James Monroe on the attack on the Chesapeake, with Monroe's letters to the Secretary of State (No. II of the papers laid before Congress), counted by its first document, Canning's note of 25 July 1807 on the first news of the attack.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Rose and Madison on Rose's mission
new_groups.definition: Printings of the correspondence between George Rose, the British envoy, and James Madison, Secretary of State (No. III of the papers laid before Congress), counted by its first letter: Rose's of 26 January 1808, that his instructions forbade any negotiation while the President's proclamation of 2 July 1807 remained in force; with Madison's answer of 5 March and Rose's reply of 17 March.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Champagny to Armstrong, 15 January 1808
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of the French foreign minister, Champagny, to General Armstrong, the American minister (Paris, 15 January 1808), made public by Congress on 2 April: the Emperor considered war as existing between England and the United States from the day England published her decrees, and had 'no doubt of a declaration of war against her by the United States'. It is France's own document.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The embargo at home, spring 1808
new_groups.definition: Reports and executive documents on the embargo's working in April and May 1808: a Georgia letter on its effect at Mobile and Pensacola, the President's proclamation on Lake Champlain, and his letter to five governors on supplies of flour. Contains those three groups; the grouping is by subject.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A Georgia letter: Mobile and Pensacola
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Georgia (14 March 1808): the embargo had left the citizens of Mobile and Pensacola 'almost in a state of starvation', with the prices of corn and flour there. It is one unnamed correspondent's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's proclamation on Lake Champlain
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's proclamation of 19 April 1808: persons on Lake Champlain and the adjacent country were combining to obstruct the embargo laws, too strong for the ordinary course of justice, and were commanded to disperse. It alleges insurrection; several papers printed it from the Rutland Herald of 30 April.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's letter to the governors on flour
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's letter of 6 May 1808 to the governors of Orleans, Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and New Hampshire: since shipments of flour had become generally suspicious, the governors might certify merchants they trusted to bring in flour for the needs of their states.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Revolution in Spain: two letters from Alicante
new_groups.definition: Two letters from Alicante, both dated 27 March 1808, on the rising at Aranjuez and the fall of the Prince of Peace, as American papers printed them in May 1808, several of them side by side ('Extract of another Letter'). Contains those two groups. Each is one letter-writer's account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Alicante letter: 'a rumour being spread at Aranjuez'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, received at Boston and introduced as 'interesting particulars of the affairs of Spain': a rumour that the royal family meant to leave for Cadiz and embark on the English squadron brought crowds to the palace at Aranjuez; the Prince of Peace fell, and the King resigned his crown to his son. One paper prints only its later part.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Alicante letter: the guards ordered to Aranjuez
new_groups.definition: Printings of another letter from Alicante of 27 March 1808, which reached Boston by the brig Sally: on the evening of 18 March the Prince of Peace ordered the Spanish and Walloon guards to Aranjuez; a report that the royal family meant to flee to Gibraltar and America brought a crowd to the palace crying 'kill the traitor'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: John Quincy Adams resigns from the Senate
new_groups.definition: Printings of John Quincy Adams's letter of 8 June 1808 to the Massachusetts legislature, resigning his seat in the Senate after the legislature had passed resolutions disapproving of measures he had supported.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Charles IV names Murat lieutenant-general of Spain
new_groups.definition: Printings of Charles IV's letter to Murat, 'Brother, my absence and infirmities…', enclosing the royal decree (Bayonne, 4 May 1808) that made him lieutenant-general of the kingdom, to govern in the King's name. A document issued under French control.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British order in council of 4 July: peace with Spain
new_groups.definition: Printings of the order of the King in Council of 4 July 1808: in view of the Spanish nation's 'glorious exertions' against France, all hostilities against Spain were to cease, the blockade of Spanish ports not held by France was raised, and Spanish vessels were admitted to British ports.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Canning in the Commons on America, 24 June
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report of George Canning's remarks in the House of Commons on 24 June 1808, answering Mr. Whitbread: no communication had come from the American government since Mr. Rose's return; he could only conjecture that America was negotiating with France; reparation for the Chesapeake had been offered without giving up the right of search. The papers' heading calls him the Prime Minister; he was Foreign Secretary.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Jefferson's answer to the New Hampshire legislature
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the address of the New Hampshire legislature of 14 June 1808, which had approved the measures of his administration, the embargo among them.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: News from Spain by the Arcturus
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston Gazette report of 5 September 1808: the ship Arcturus, 48 days from St. Sebastian, had arrived with P. R. Livingston, bearer of dispatches from the French government, and with passengers' accounts that General Dupont had been defeated at Cordova and Andujar. A report from passengers ('is said').
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Jefferson's answer to the petitions against the embargo
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's answer to the petition of the Boston town meeting, which had asked him to suspend the embargo: he could not suspend it while the belligerents' edicts stood, and only the legislature could prescribe its course. The Portland Gazette prints the same text as the answer to Portland's petition.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Reding's dispatch on the battle of Baylen
new_groups.definition: Printings of the dispatch of the Spanish general Reding to General Castaños, 22 July 1808, on the action of 19 July near Baylen, in which Dupont attacked the Spanish camp; printed from Spanish papers. One army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The conventions in Portugal, 1808
new_groups.definition: The two conventions of late August and early September 1808 that ended the French occupation of Portugal, as American papers printed them from London papers in October and November: the surrender of the Russian fleet in the Tagus, and the evacuation of Portugal by the French army. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The convention for the Russian fleet in the Tagus
new_groups.definition: Printings of the articles agreed on 3 September 1808 between the Russian Vice-Admiral Seniavin and Admiral Sir Charles Cotton for the surrender of the Russian fleet in the Tagus, to be held by Britain until after a peace, with Cotton's covering letter.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The convention for the evacuation of Portugal
new_groups.definition: Printings of the definitive convention of 30 August 1808 (the Convention of Cintra) between the British and French commanders in Portugal: the French army was to leave Portugal and be carried to France in British ships.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 8 November and its documents
new_groups.definition: President Jefferson's last annual message, at the opening of the second session of the Tenth Congress on 8 November 1808, and three of the diplomatic papers sent with it, which the papers printed in later issues and in instalments: Canning's note to Pinkney, an extract of Armstrong's letter from France, and Madison's letter to Erskine. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 8 November
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 8 November 1808: the overtures to Britain and France had failed, their edicts stood, and Congress was to decide what course to take on the embargo.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Canning's answer to Pinkney, 23 September
new_groups.definition: Printings of George Canning's note to William Pinkney (Foreign Office, 23 September 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: Britain declined the American offer to suspend the embargo as to Britain if the Orders in Council were withdrawn. The British side's own statement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Armstrong to Madison, 28 August
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of General Armstrong's letter to the Secretary of State from Bourbon l'Archambault, 28 August 1808, sent to Congress with the President's message: he would not return to Paris to renew his discussions with Champagny, being convinced that a new attempt would be useless and probably injurious.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Madison to Erskine on the Orders in Council, 25 March
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's letter to David Erskine, the British minister (25 March 1808), sent to Congress with the President's message: the Orders in Council of November 1807 could not be justified as retaliation for the French decrees.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The House committee's report on foreign relations
new_groups.definition: Printings of the report in part of the House committee on the part of the President's message concerning foreign relations (presented on 22 November 1808 by George W. Campbell): the choice lay between submission, war with both Britain and France, and continuing the embargo with stricter enforcement; with three resolutions.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1808 that reach 4 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 125 items in 7 or more papers). Because several of the year's most printed documents sit in families that began in 1807, the same script was also run with year 1807 over the 1808 pages (items_from_1807.json: 54 items in 7 or more papers). Two AI reviewers read the items of each half of the year and proposed the stories; each item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 4,466 pages of 1808 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit was read. Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched with loose keywords, and the scan pages whose RevX text is filed under another page were read in the CA transcription. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776 and 1807: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs and items that need framing. Items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months and the main kinds of news. Stories are counted item by item; where one publication holds several documents, or several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent story reaches 7 (the rule the owner agreed for 1776 round two). A paper that printed an item again later counts each printing. Kentucky Gazette pages filed under 1808 are 1806 issues and were not used.

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder joins the embargo acts into chains (one item reaches 11 papers and 110 printings) because each supplementary act names the act it supplements and all share the enacting formula. Each act was counted by its own first section: the Embargo Act 5 papers in 1808, the act of 9 January 6, of 12 March 5, of 22 April 7, of 25 April 6. Bills printed before the acts were not counted, except a bill as passed by the Senate whose text is the act's (ADA 9 January; WR 5 May).
counted_item_by_item.The two Alicante letters: Two letters from Alicante, both dated 27 March 1808, were printed side by side (VA: 'Extract of another Letter'). The reviewers first took them for two parts of one letter in 8 papers; by their own wording each is in 7 papers, and each is its own group.
counted_item_by_item.The papers laid before Congress in March: About 45 items in the item lists are parts of one publication. They were grouped by the publication's own parts (the message; No. II, Canning and Monroe; No. III, Rose and Madison) and Champagny's letter, published separately on 2 April, each counted by its first document.
counted_item_by_item.Canning's speech of 24 June: Printed in two forms, a report ('The following observations were made by Mr. Canning…', 4 papers) and an 'Extract from Mr. Canning's speech' in his own words (3 papers); counted together as one speech, 7 papers.
counted_item_by_item.Jefferson's answer to the petitions: The same text was sent to several towns: 6 papers print the answer to Boston and the Portland Gazette the answer to Portland. Counted together, 7 papers.
counted_item_by_item.Commentary and debates: Pages that only quote an item (editorials, speeches, debate reports, later orders that recite an earlier one) were not counted: for example Campbell's report quoted in the Portland Gazette, Canning's letter of 23 September read out in Congress, the Orders in Council quoted in essays.

for_user_decision.The Embargo Act's December 1807 printing: The act was first printed in late December 1807 (5 papers by the 1807 count). The site requires every printing of a reviewed year's group to fall in that year, so the 1808 group holds its 5 January printings only; across both years the act reaches 8 papers.
for_user_decision.Sub-stories below 7 papers: Four embargo laws (5, 6, 5, 6), the Order in Council of 11 November 1807 (6), the Cintra convention (6) and Canning's answer to Pinkney (6; the Enquirer says it printed it on 15 November, an issue the collection lacks), under parents that reach 7 or more.
for_user_decision.Two parents grouped by subject: 'Orders and decrees against neutral trade' and 'The embargo at home, spring 1808' group separate documents by subject.
for_user_decision.Two printed forms counted together: Canning's speech of 24 June (report and extract) and the President's answer to the petitions (to Boston and to Portland).
for_user_decision.The 'Melancholy Event' near Burlington,: Men of a revenue party killed by smugglers while enforcing the embargo; it names the dead and, later, the accused. Left out for framing.
for_user_decision.General Wilkinson's letters to Robert Go: A quarrel of honour published by Wilkinson. Left out.
for_user_decision.Governor Sevier's letter on the Creeks (: Needs framing first, like the Cherokee and Creek reports of 1776. Left out.
for_user_decision.Allegations in the Wilkinson story: Clark's statement and the Wilkinson-Randolph letters are allegations and personal attacks between public men in a public affair; the court of inquiry found no evidence. Admitted with the claims labelled.

data_issues.Kentucky Gazette issues filed two years: The 98 issues of sn84038147 filed under 1808 print 1806 in their mastheads (87 readable; the masthead weekday fits 1806); the 7 filed under 1806 are 1804 and the one filed 28 May 1807 is 1805. No 1808 story uses them. Evidence: outputs/story_discovery_1808/check_kentucky_gazette_dates.py and kentucky_gazette_dates.csv.
